strengths: Clear identification and validation of perception as the bottleneck in abstract visual reasoning, with compelling empirical evidence across 17 MLLMs
Comprehensive benchmark design with systematic coverage of five core perceptual dimensions grounded in cognitive science, addressing a gap in existing evaluations
Well-documented data collection and quality control pipeline with 12 trained annotators ensuring high-quality benchmark construction
Extensive experimental evaluation showing perceptual supervision significantly improves performance (43.7% vs 20.9% baseline) without architectural changes
Automated synthesis framework (PRS) provides a scalable approach to generating training data with intermediate supervision, demonstrated to be more effective than reasoning-only approaches
Rigorous demonstration that scaling approaches and CoT prompting alone cannot solve AVR tasks without addressing perception
weaknesses: Critical experimental gap: ablation study validating perceptual supervision (Table 4) conducted only on synthetic data subset, not on actual VisuRiddles benchmark—domain transfer not demonstrated

Limited conceptual novelty: benchmark primarily consolidates existing civil service exam problems; five dimensions are established in prior cognitive science work; RAVEN/Sudoku are incorporated existing benchmarks
Insufficient analysis of synthetic-to-real domain gap: models trained on rule-based synthetic data with explicit annotations; unclear how perceptual descriptions help on unannotated real data
Incomplete failure analysis: only one case study provided; 'Other' category shows unexpected negative improvements with more data (-1.9% to -0.4%) left unexplained; no systematic error breakdown

Benchmark size concerns: 1000 total samples (800 in basic categories), modest for comprehensive evaluation; 'Other' category poorly defined; perfectly balanced answer distributions may not reflect natural difficulty

Underspecified technical details: how are 'plausible distractors' generated; justification for 34 sub-rules unclear; no comparison with alternative supervision strategies or human-written descriptions
Limited generalization evidence: all evaluated models are VLMs; no cross-dataset evaluation on other benchmarks; applicability to other visual reasoning tasks unclear

Claim validation incomplete: while perceptual supervision helps, alternative explanations not ruled out (e.g., regularization effects, data volume, model capacity); causality not definitively established

strengths: Clear problem identification with compelling evidence (Figure 1b) that structured perceptual descriptions enable models to solve problems they fail on with raw images
Comprehensive benchmark with 1,000 carefully curated AVR problems from real exams, covering 8 diverse reasoning categories with structured quality control
Strong ablation studies (Tables 3-4) convincingly demonstrate perception bottleneck: GPT-4o improves from 27.6% to 60.1%, Qwen2.5VL from 30.9% to 73.6% with descriptions
Well-designed synthesizer that automatically generates 20K+ training instances with aligned perceptual descriptions across modular rule categories
Extensive empirical evaluation across 17+ models (11 open-source, 6 commercial) with clear performance improvements
Good visualization and interpretability (Figures 4-5) illustrating failure modes and the model's rethinking phenomenon
Planned public release of benchmark and code will benefit the community
weaknesses: Critical comparison fairness issue: Only PAVR is fine-tuned on synthetic data; all baselines use zero-shot/CoT. Unclear whether improvements stem from perception-augmentation or domain-specific fine-tuning. Missing control: fine-tuning baselines on same synthetic data without perceptual descriptions

Limited generalization: Results on VisuLogic (30.6%) are only marginally better than some baselines (InternVL2.5-38B-RL: 31.1%), raising questions about whether gains are specific to VisuRiddles-style problems

Dataset scale and diversity constraints: Only 1,000 samples with single source (Chinese civil service exams); acknowledged in paper that rule design and icon library are restricted, limiting diversity of synthesized data

Technical novelty is limited: Two-stage SFT+RL approach is not novel; concurrent work on similar methods (R1-OneVision, Visual-RFT). Perceptual descriptions are orthogonal to the core insight about fine-grained perception

Incomplete disentanglement of perception vs. reasoning: Table 3 uses synthetically-generated data (simpler than real benchmark); no analysis of failure modes or cases where better perception doesn't enable correct reasoning
Statistical rigor lacking: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or inter-annotator agreement reporting. Figure 5's 'rethinking' phenomenon observed but not quantified
Generalization not tested beyond AVR: Only evaluated on 2 AVR benchmarks; unclear if perception augmentation helps on other visual reasoning tasks
Large gap to human performance remains (46.8% vs. 63.0%), indicating PAVR still falls substantially short of human-level performance
